title: Status Epilepticus and Acute Seizures: ED Stabilisation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult convulsive status epilepticus in the emergency department (ED). Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) first-aid advice informs immediate safety actions and the 5-minute escalation threshold; no Saudi adult hospital dosing protocol was located. International guidance is labelled as a gap-filler for hospital pharmacotherapy.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi adult hospital protocol with antiseizure-medicine doses was located in the Saudi Ministry of Health protocol catalogue or Saudi Epilepsy Society clinical-guideline page on 18 October 2026. International guidance remains a gap-filler and must not be represented as Saudi endorsement.
The Saudi MOH source is public first-aid guidance, not an adult emergency-department prescribing protocol.

The International guideline doses require Saudi clinician and hospital-formulary review before local adoption; Saudi Food and Drug Authority registration was not verified because the register could not be accessed.

The opened 2025 Intensive Care Society guidance says patients with severe renal or liver impairment and most adults over 65 years were excluded from the ESETT dosing evidence; it does not supply a complete adjustment schedule for every medicine.
Pregnancy-specific treatment is outside this adult non-obstetric guideline; suspected eclampsia needs the obstetric emergency pathway.
Non-convulsive status epilepticus, paediatric care, exact dextrose/thiamine treatment and local transfer/discharge arrangements require separately verified Saudi protocols.
Continuous infusion regimens retained from the prior version require source-table re-verification before clinician approval.

pathophysiology.summary: Status epilepticus is continuous seizure activity for 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness; treatment must start early. Generalised convulsive status epilepticus threatens airway, oxygenation and circulation and requires immediate emergency treatment. A benzodiazepine is first-line treatment; a non-benzodiazepine antiseizure medicine follows when seizures continue after two benzodiazepine doses. Refractory status epilepticus persists after one benzodiazepine and one non-benzodiazepine antiseizure medicine and requires critical-care admission and intravenous anaesthesia.

symptoms: Tonic-clonic movements lasting 5 minutes or more.
Repeated seizures without recovery between them.
physicalSigns: Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia or hypotension on first check.
redFlags: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness.
Airway, breathing or circulatory compromise; persistent depressed consciousness; or need for intubation.
Failure of two benzodiazepine doses or ongoing seizure after a second-line antiseizure medicine.
Pregnancy, suspected central nervous system infection, acute head injury, stroke, toxic exposure or severe metabolic disturbance.
precipitants: Alcohol or drug withdrawal or toxicity.

Altered mental state without convulsion; continuous EEG within 1 hour of suspicion.
Pregnancy with severe hypertension; use magnesium sulfate.

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise
actions: Time the seizure; protect from injury, remove hazards, do not restrain the patient and do not place anything in the mouth. These are Saudi MOH first-aid actions.
Position the airway, give oxygen, assess vital signs and capillary glucose, and establish intravenous access while resuscitation continues.
After convulsions end, place the patient in the recovery position and remain with them until recovered; activate emergency transfer for a seizure longer than 5 minutes or breathing difficulty.

clinicalManagement.title: First-line benzodiazepine
actions: IV lorazepam 4 mg (0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg per dose), repeat once in 5–10 minutes; or IM midazolam 10 mg; or IV diazepam 10 mg (0.15 mg/kg), repeat once.
Give an adequate single full dose, not split small doses.
Without IV access: IM midazolam, or buccal or rectal options per local protocol.

clinicalManagement.title: Second-line antiseizure medicine
clinicalManagement.timeframe: From 5–10 minutes after the first benzodiazepine dose (NCS); AES second therapy starts at 20 minutes
actions: After two benzodiazepine doses, seek expert guidance and give intravenous levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate. NICE identifies these alternatives but does not specify doses.

The 2025 Intensive Care Society gap-filler doses are levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4.5 g), sodium valproate 40 mg/kg IV (maximum 3 g), or phenytoin/fosphenytoin 15–20 mg/kg IV (maximum 2 g); use only after Saudi clinician and formulary review.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory status epilepticus
actions: Seek expert guidance; consider an alternative second-line drug or phenobarbital or general anaesthesia (NG217).
NCS infusions: midazolam bolus 0.2 mg/kg then 0.05–2 mg/kg per hour, or propofol 1–2 mg/kg load then 30–200 µg/kg per minute.
Admit to the intensive care unit (ICU) with continuous EEG; titrate to EEG endpoints.

clinicalManagement.title: Find the cause
actions: Send blood tests, consider head CT, lumbar puncture and toxicology by presentation.
Treat the cause; consider vasopressors if systolic pressure is below 90 mmHg.

regimens.dose: 0.1 mg/kg IV or intraosseous (IO), maximum 4 mg
regimens.frequency: Give immediately at 5 minutes; a second benzodiazepine dose may be given if the seizure continues 5–10 minutes after the first dose.
regimens.duration: Two doses at most before second-line
adjustments: For weight below 50 kg or age above 70 years, give 1–2 mg aliquots (ICS Appendix 3).
No complete renal, hepatic or pregnancy adjustment schedule was verified; seek pharmacist and specialist advice.
monitoring: Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure.
contraindications: Respiratory depression risk; contraindications not listed in the source.

regimens.frequency: Single loading dose after two benzodiazepine doses; maintenance 20–30 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses, 8 hours after the loading dose.

medicationPlan.note: Saudi MOH guidance supports first-aid safety actions and escalation for seizures lasting longer than 5 minutes; it does not provide adult hospital drug doses. The doses below are international gap-fillers and are not Saudi-endorsed. Check the hospital formulary and involve emergency, neurology and critical-care teams.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: If seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first dose (NG217).

patientEducation: Tell the family to time future seizures, protect the person from injury, avoid restraint and objects in the mouth, and call emergency services for a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or breathing difficulty.
After a seizure ends, use the recovery position, stay with the person until they have recovered and arrange individualised emergency planning with neurology.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid triggers such as sleep deprivation and alcohol; adhere to antiseizure medicine.
mdtReferrals: Neurology; critical care; emergency medicine; neurophysiology for EEG; pharmacy.
dischargeCriteria: Do not discharge during ongoing seizure activity, persistent altered consciousness, respiratory compromise, an unexplained first seizure, recurrent seizures, abnormal investigation requiring treatment or without a safe neurology plan.
Discharge criteria and follow-up timing need a locally verified Saudi emergency-department protocol and neurology decision; this remains unverified.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange neurology review and an individualised emergency management plan. Verify Saudi driving, work-safety and follow-up requirements locally; they were not verified in the opened sources.
